title: Three Indian Americans Named to TIME100 Philanthropy List — and Their Work Is Reshaping How the Diaspora Gives
excerpt: Rajiv Shah, Deepak Bhargava, and Anna Verghese represent a new generation of Indian-American philanthropic leadership that goes far beyond writing cheques
body:
Three Indian Americans have been named to TIME magazine's 2026 TIME100 Philanthropy list, a recognition that signals something larger than individual achievement: the Indian-American community is no longer just a beneficiary of American opportunity — it is actively reshaping the infrastructure of global giving.

## The Honourees

**Rajiv J. Shah**, president of the Rockefeller Foundation and the first Indian American to lead the 112-year-old institution, was recognised for his work directing philanthropic initiatives across global health, climate resilience, food security and economic opportunity. A physician and economist born in Detroit to Gujarati immigrant parents, Shah previously served as administrator of USAID under President Obama, where he oversaw the American response to the 2010 Haiti earthquake and the Ebola crisis.

"We need to work with faith-based institutions, and heads of state, government officials, with entrepreneurs, with academic scientists," Shah told TIME. "It's through these kinds of broad partnerships that we are able to really make a difference."

**Deepak Bhargava**, president of Freedom Together — one of the largest progressive grant-making organisations in the United States — was recognised for directing funding toward racial equity, immigrant rights, democracy-building and economic justice. A veteran organiser who previously led the Center for Community Change for over a decade, Bhargava has spent his career building coalitions that bridge the gap between policy advocacy and grassroots power.

"We are at an inflection… with severe challenges to fundamental rights, the rule of law, and basic norms," Bhargava said. "That demands an extraordinary response."

**Anna Verghese**, executive director of The Audacious Project — a TED-created philanthropic platform — was honoured for helping mobilise more than $8 billion in multi-year, unrestricted funding for 70 projects worldwide. Her work represents a newer model of collaborative philanthropy that pools resources across foundations, families and individuals to back high-impact ventures at scale.

## Beyond the Temple Donation Box

The three honourees represent a marked evolution in Indian-American philanthropy. For decades, diaspora giving was largely channelled through religious institutions, hometown associations and disaster-relief campaigns. While those traditions remain vital, a growing cohort of Indian Americans is now occupying leadership positions at some of the world's most influential philanthropic institutions — shaping not just where money flows but how the entire sector operates.

The numbers tell part of the story. Indian Americans, who make up roughly 1.5 per cent of the US population, have a median household income of over $150,000 — the highest of any ethnic group in the country. That wealth is increasingly translating into structured, institutional philanthropy rather than purely informal giving.

The Rockefeller Foundation under Shah has committed over $1 billion to climate and health initiatives since 2020. Freedom Together under Bhargava distributed more than $200 million in its first three years. The Audacious Project under Verghese has backed initiatives ranging from malaria vaccine distribution to ocean conservation.

## The Diaspora Angle

For NRIs watching from afar, these appointments carry particular resonance. Indian-origin leaders at the helm of American philanthropic institutions signal a community that has moved beyond the model-minority narrative of professional success into positions of genuine institutional power.

The recognition also comes at a politically charged moment. As debates around immigration, H-1B visas and the role of immigrants in American life intensify, the TIME100 Philanthropy list offers a counter-narrative: Indian Americans not merely succeeding in America but actively reinvesting in its social fabric.

TIME introduced the TIME100 Philanthropy list in 2025 to spotlight individuals influencing charitable giving and nonprofit innovation worldwide. The 2026 edition includes philanthropists, activists and public figures from several countries — but the three Indian-American honourees stand out for the breadth and ambition of their work.

## What Comes Next

The question for the broader diaspora is whether this institutional presence will translate into deeper engagement with India-specific challenges. Shah's Rockefeller Foundation has significant programmes in India; Bhargava's immigrant-rights work directly affects the diaspora; Verghese's platform has backed India-focused projects.

As Indian Americans continue to ascend in American philanthropy, the opportunity — and the expectation — is that this influence will flow in both directions, connecting the resources and networks of the diaspora with the needs of a country that sent them forth.
